Repeated exposure to hot contexts (with appropriate scaffolding) may build robustness. Stress inoculation training, graduated exposure to performance pressure, and simulation-based practice under arousal all attempt to shift the threshold at which control degrades. The mechanism may involve both (a) habituation (reduced physiological reactivity to formerly-alarming cues) and (b) proceduralizing coping strategies until they can execute under load. This suggests that controlled exposure to manageable hot contexts may be more developmentally productive than either overprotection (no exposure, leaving the system untrained) or overwhelming exposure (unmanageable arousal that produces avoidance, learned helplessness, or traumatic encoding).

What promotes post-formal development? These capacities are not automatic with age; they require what might be called optimal marginality–repeated exposure to problems that cannot be solved within the current cognitive framework, under conditions that support growth rather than defensive regression. Key environmental features include: (a) genuine exposure to different perspectives that are held by intelligent people for intelligible reasons (not strawmen or out-group caricatures); (b) ill-structured problems where the "right answer" cannot be looked up and reasonable people disagree; (c) feedback that is delayed, noisy, and requires effortful causal attribution rather than immediate and unambiguous; (d) mentorship, dialogue partners, or cultural models who demonstrate post-formal reasoning in action; and (e) sufficient psychological safety to tolerate the discomfort of uncertainty without retreating into rigid positions. Professional training in medicine, law, engineering, scientific research, and complex management often provides these conditions; many other life paths do not. This explains why post-formal reasoning is correlated with–but not guaranteed by–higher education: it is not the credential but the exposure to a specific kind of cognitive environment that matters.
